opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I don't think I've completely figured it out. The way I think about it is that I don't treat them as three separate jobs competing for my time. They're really connected by one theme, which is building machine learning systems that make AI more accessible and efficient.

On the research side, a lot of what I do is open source, projects like XGBoost, TVM, and more recently the work on running models efficiently on all kinds of devices. Those projects naturally connect research and real-world impact. When we build something in the lab and people start using it, we learn what the real problems are, and that feeds back into new research questions. The startup side is a continuation of that. It's a way to take some of those ideas and make sure they reach people at scale.

Practically, a few things help me. First, I rely a lot on working with great people. As a faculty member, my students are the core of the research. My job is less about writing every line of code myself and more about helping them find good problems, giving feedback, and making sure they grow. The same is true in the startup context. You have to trust the team.

Second, I try to protect blocks of time for deep thinking. It's easy to fill your day with meetings and context switching, but the most valuable things usually come from sitting down and thinking hard about one problem. So I try to be intentional about that.

Third, I accept that the balance shifts over time. Some months a paper deadline or a teaching term takes priority, and some months something in the open source community or the company needs more attention. Instead of trying to make every week perfectly balanced, I ask whether, over a longer period, I'm moving the things I care about forward.

And finally, I enjoy it. Building systems, seeing people use them, and working with students is what I love doing. When the work is something you're genuinely excited about, it feels less like managing time and more like following your curiosity, just with a lot of help from good collaborators.

r002.rationale: It says he trusts the startup team, but does not explain limiting his involvement to high-level technical work to preserve time for other responsibilities.

r003.rationale: It describes students as central and his role as guiding and supporting them, but does not say they are independently driven or connect that independence to his supporting role.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of them as three separate buckets competing for my time. For me, they're really one thing viewed from different angles, and that's deliberate.

Most of my research is about building systems that make machine learning actually usable in the real world. Projects like XGBoost, TVM, and MLC LLM came out of the question: how do we make this efficient enough and accessible enough that people can actually deploy it? That same question is at the heart of the startup. So when I spend a day on OctoAI problems, I'm usually seeing the exact pain points that then inform what my students and I work on at CMU. And when a student comes up with a new compiler technique or a new way to run models on edge devices, that feeds back into the open-source project, which the company builds on. It's a loop, not a split.

The faculty role is where I get to think longer-term and work with people who aren't constrained by this quarter's roadmap. That's incredibly valuable, because a company naturally pulls you toward what's needed now, and a university pulls you toward what might matter in five years. Having both keeps me honest in both directions.

That said, there are some practical things I do. I try to be very intentional about what I personally go deep on. I can't touch everything, so I pick a small number of technical problems where I think my hands-on involvement makes a real difference, and I try to empower other people to own everything else. Open source helps a lot here, because the community and the team carry a lot of the load, and my job becomes more about setting direction and removing obstacles.

I also try to protect time for actually writing code. It's easy for someone in my position to drift entirely into meetings and advising, and then you lose touch with what's actually hard. Staying close to the implementation is how I keep my intuition sharp, and frankly it's the part I enjoy most.

So the short answer is: I try to align the three so they reinforce each other rather than compete, and then I'm pretty ruthless about focusing my own attention on the few places where it matters most.

astra-6.text:
I think about it less as dividing my time into three separate buckets and more as finding a common thread. Research, working with students, and being involved in a startup can all inform one another. A practical problem can lead to a research question, and a research idea can open up something useful in practice.

Of course, that doesn’t eliminate the tradeoffs. I try to ask where my involvement is most useful at a particular moment, and where other people should have the space to take ownership. You need uninterrupted time to think, but you also need to be available to the people you work with.

I wouldn’t say there’s a perfect balance. It’s an ongoing process of choosing priorities and being realistic about what you can commit to.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as connected rather than as three completely separate jobs. Research is about finding important problems and exploring ideas. The faculty role includes helping students develop their own judgment and become independent researchers. And startup involvement brings a different perspective: what does it take for an idea to become something people can actually use?

Of course, those connections don’t remove the time constraint. You still have to choose where your attention matters most. My approach is to keep a small number of priorities and be comfortable saying no to other things. And you need to give people ownership. If every decision depends on you, then your time becomes the bottleneck.

I don’t think there’s a perfect balance every day. It’s more about whether, over time, these activities reinforce each other and whether you’re spending your energy on the things where you can contribute most.
